chapter: RCA years: Rollins, Nero and singers
title: Creating Peter Nero at RCA
summary: He renamed Bernie Nierow as a suave pop pianist, borrowing Bette Davis's 'Petah'.

story.theme_name: How I got my name: nicknames and band monikers
story.community_name: How I got my name: nicknames and band names

blocks.x: Nierow doesn’t exactly stack up as a commercial name.” He was quite amenable. He understood immediately. I said, “The Nierow part is okay. We’ll spell it N-e-r-o, but Bernie Nierow doesn’t sound like the kind of pianist that we want you to be, very sophisticated, suave, playing show tunes and the usual thing.” I’d had an incredible success with Liberace at Columbia, but that was really Paul Weston’s story. That’s a great story, which I hope we have time to tell, because Liberace was signed – no, I’m not going to tell the story. You’ve found already, my stories have stories within stories. They hang together.
Do you want to finish with Bernie?

Yeah. With Bernie, the question was, what kind of name can we get? Then I thought about the classic thing that everybody did in doing takeoffs on Bette Davis. They always had that line about, “Peter, Peter, come here. Peter,” and so forth.

Yeah, Petah. Bette Davis had told me that she never did a movie in her life in which there was anybody named Peter, but this is the thing everybody picked up on. But I thought, Peter Nero. This has all the sophistication that you connect with Bette Davis and show people and so forth, and it worked beautifully. So, end of story.
